explanations.explanation: That's Julius, a centurion who belonged to the Imperial Regiment (Acts 27:1). Paul and the other prisoners get handed over to him for the trip to Italy. He turns up again in this very passage, so keep his name handy, friend. A centurion is a Roman officer, and this one now has a boatload of prisoners to look after.

Cornelius is a different centurion, one in Caesarea (Acts 10:1). Easy to mix up, since centurions pop up all over the Bible and none of them wear name tags. The man who gets Paul and the other prisoners here is Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment (Acts 27:1). Same job, different guy, friend.

Festus is the one Paul was talking to when he said, "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11). Now the trip to Italy is on, and Acts 27:1 says Paul and some other prisoners are handed over to a centurion named Julius. So Festus already had his turn with Paul, and Julius has the next one. Julius is the name to remember, friend.

True, and the text says it plainly: "Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care" (Acts 27:3). I spent years in a cramped junk drawer, so a day out with friends sounds like a vacation to me. I think a prisoner getting that visit is a real kindness. Julius gets a little credit here, baker.

Not this time. Acts 27:3 says "Julius treated Paul with consideration, allowing him to visit his friends and receive their care." So the centurion allows the visit, and Paul receives their care. I think that's a real kindness, baker, and a nice stop before the sea turns rough.

Winds it is: "the winds were against us" (Acts 27:4). So they sail to the lee of Cyprus, the sheltered side, instead of pushing straight across. Sometimes the smart move is to stop arguing with the weather, friend.

Pirates would make a juicy story, but the text never mentions any here. Acts 27:4 says "the winds were against us." That's what sends them to the lee of Cyprus, the sheltered side. This crew only has weather to deal with in this verse, friend.

Currents sound reasonable, friend, but that's not what the writer puts down. Acts 27:4 says "the winds were against us." Nothing about currents shows up in that verse. The wind is what pushes them to the lee of Cyprus.

Alexandria is the one: "the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board" (Acts 27:6). Their first ship was only headed for ports along the coast of Asia (Acts 27:2). This one is going to Italy, which is the whole point of the trip. That's like finally catching the direct flight after a pile of connections.

Nice guess, but Tyre isn't on this ticket. Acts 27:6 says Julius found "an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy." So the ship comes from Alexandria, and Julius is the one who finds it. Tyre will have to sit this one out, friend.

Joppa is a real place in the Bible, but this verse doesn't use it. Acts 27:6 says the centurion found "an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy" and put them on board. So the ship is from Alexandria. Joppa will have to sit this one out, baker.

Easy would have been nice, friend, but that isn't what the text says. Acts 27:8 says they "moved along the coast with difficulty" before they reached Fair Havens. So the sailing is still a struggle. Smooth sailing isn't in the forecast yet.

It's false, baker. Acts 27:8 says they "moved along the coast with difficulty" before they came to Fair Havens. So even along Crete, the going is still hard. Nobody on that boat was kicking back with a cookie yet.

explanations.answer: Disaster and great loss even of their lives
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well" (Acts 27:10). Verse 9 had just said the voyage was already dangerous. Paul doesn't say "might get a little bumpy," friend. He says lives.

explanations.answer: A long delay but no real danger
explanations.explanation: That's way softer than what Paul says. In Acts 27:10 he says the voyage will be filled with "disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well." Verse 9 had already said the voyage was dangerous. A delay would be an inconvenience, friend, but Paul sees lives at stake.

explanations.answer: A sickness spreading among the prisoners
explanations.explanation: Sickness doesn't show up in this passage. What Paul says is "disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well" (Acts 27:10). He's talking about the voyage itself, friend. No bug going around the boat.

Julius doesn't go along with it. Acts 27:11 says, "contrary to Paul’s advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship." Paul gets the warning out, and it lands in the unread pile.

It's false, friend. "Contrary to Paul’s advice, the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). You know when you give somebody directions and they follow the GPS anyway? Paul knows that feeling.

Pilot is right: "the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship" (Acts 27:11). The text doesn't tell us what they said, only that Julius was persuaded. So the ship's pilot and its owner get Julius's ear, and Paul's warning gets set aside.

Soldiers make sense, since Julius is a centurion, but the text says "pilot" (Acts 27:11). The pilot and the owner of the ship are the ones who persuade him. This verse doesn't mention soldiers at all, friend.

Prisoners? Friend, they're the ones with no say in the matter. Acts 27:11 says "the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and by the owner of the ship." Paul is a prisoner too (Acts 27:1), and he's the one Julius doesn't follow.

explanations.answer: The harbor isn't good for spending winter
explanations.explanation: That's the reason: "Since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to sail on" (Acts 27:12). So they're not sailing off to nowhere. They hope to reach Phoenix and winter there. Nobody wants to spend a whole winter somewhere that doesn't work, like an oven that only heats one corner.

explanations.answer: The town of Lasea won't let them stay
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Lasea turns them away. Lasea is just the town near Fair Havens (Acts 27:8). The reason in Acts 27:12 is that "the harbor was unsuitable to winter in." No town slammed a door on anybody, friend.

explanations.answer: Paul tells them the weather will hold
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Paul says. In Acts 27:10 he warns of "disaster and great loss." Later he says they should have followed his advice not to sail from Crete (Acts 27:21). The majority wanted to sail on because "the harbor was unsuitable to winter in" (Acts 27:12), so Paul's the one who'd rather not.

Yes, the Northeaster: "it was not long before a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island" (Acts 27:14). Not long after that gentle south wind, friend. That wind had a very short career.

explanations.answer: A hailstorm like the one in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Hail did fall on Egypt, but that's a different day and a different place (Exodus 9:23). The storm here is "a cyclone called the Northeaster" that "swept down across the island" (Acts 27:14). Hail is a fine guess, baker, but the text names the wind.

explanations.answer: A whirlwind out of the desert
explanations.explanation: No desert in this one, friend. The text says "a cyclone called the Northeaster swept down across the island" (Acts 27:14). It sweeps down across Crete, so this is a sea story, not a sand story. Nobody on that ship is packing sunscreen.
Not quite. Acts 27:16 says, "we barely managed to secure the lifeboat." Barely is a word that comes with sweaty palms, friend. That was a close one by the small island of Cauda.

False, and the word to watch is "barely": "we barely managed to secure the lifeboat" (Acts 27:16). I bet it took everybody's grip. I've fumbled a cookie sheet on a calm day, so wrestling a lifeboat in a cyclone? Respect.

explanations.answer: They pass ropes under the ship
explanations.explanation: Ropes, friend: "the crew used ropes to undergird the ship" (Acts 27:17). That comes right after they hoist the lifeboat up. Ropes around a whole ship! I tie ribbon on a cookie box, and these men do it to a ship.

explanations.answer: They nail extra boards on the ship
explanations.explanation: The text says ropes, not boards. Acts 27:17 says "the crew used ropes to undergird the ship." There's no hammer anywhere in that verse, friend.

explanations.answer: They tie the ship to the lifeboat
explanations.explanation: That's backwards, baker. The lifeboat gets hoisted up first, and then "the crew used ropes to undergird the ship" (Acts 27:17). The ropes go on the ship itself. The lifeboat isn't being towed anywhere.

True: "On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands" (Acts 27:19). The cargo had started going over the day before (Acts 27:18). That ship is shedding stuff fast, friend.

It's false, friend. Acts 27:19 says, "On the third day, they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands." The cargo went first (Acts 27:18), then the tackle. That's some serious "I'll do it myself" energy.

explanations.answer: They lose all hope of being saved
explanations.explanation: That's the sad truth: "we abandoned all hope of being saved" (Acts 27:20). Neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and the great storm kept battering them. Nobody on that deck is smiling at the horizon, friend.

explanations.answer: They hope another ship will find them
explanations.explanation: No other ship shows up in this passage. Acts 27:20 says, "we abandoned all hope of being saved." That's about as far from "help is coming any minute" as you can get, friend.

explanations.answer: They hope Julius will find a way
explanations.explanation: Julius is in this story, but not in this verse. Acts 27:20 says, "we abandoned all hope of being saved." The text says the hope was gone, not that anyone was leaning on Julius. That's a heavy stretch of days, baker.

explanations.answer: They should have taken his advice and stayed
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says: "you should have followed my advice not to sail from Crete. Then you would have averted this disaster and loss" (Acts 27:21). I think that line's been sitting in Paul's mouth for a while. He brings it up before he gets to the good news, friend.

explanations.answer: They should have waited for a better wind
explanations.explanation: Waiting for a better wind sounds sensible, but Paul doesn't say it. He says they should have followed his advice "not to sail from Crete" (Acts 27:21). The advice was not to sail, friend. Nothing about timing the wind.

explanations.answer: They should have found a bigger ship there
explanations.explanation: A bigger ship is a fun idea, friend, but ship size never comes up. Paul says they should have followed his advice "not to sail from Crete," and that doing so "would have averted this disaster and loss" (Acts 27:21). His advice was about whether to sail, not what to sail in.

True: "you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). Paul gets this from the angel, who tells him, "God has granted you the lives of all who sail with you" (Acts 27:24). After days of no hope, that's the best news on the boat. I'd have asked him to say it twice.

It's false, baker. Paul says, "you will not experience any loss of life, but only of the ship" (Acts 22 is not it, it's Acts 27:22). So every life on board is covered. After days of lost hope, that sentence is a gift.

The ship: Paul says there will be no loss of life, "but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). So the men are safe and the ship is the one paying the price. Lose the pan, keep the bakers. That's a trade I'd take every time, friend.

The lifeboat isn't what Paul names. He says "only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). The crew did work hard to hoist the lifeboat up (Acts 27:16-17), so I get the guess, friend. But Paul's words are about the ship.
A mast never comes up, baker. Paul says there will be no loss of life, "but only of the ship" (Acts 27:22). He doesn't name any one part, a mast included. The ship is the word he uses.

That's it. The angel says, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). Caesar was the Roman emperor, and back in Acts 25:11 Paul had said, "I appeal to Caesar!" So even in that storm, the angel's words point to Caesar.

Jerusalem isn't in what the angel says. The words are "you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). And right now the boat is headed for Italy (Acts 27:1), friend. Jerusalem is nowhere on this ship's map.

That was earlier, when Julius allowed Paul to visit his friends at Sidon (Acts 27:3). The angel is talking about what's ahead: "you must stand before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). Sidon is way back on the map, friend.
Paul isn't promising a smooth landing, friend. He says, "However, we must run aground on some island" (Acts 27:26). So the ship does hit ground. That's a landing nobody's putting on a postcard.
It's false, and Paul says it plainly: "However, we must run aground on some island" (Acts 27:26). The lives are covered, but the ship runs aground. That "however" is carrying a lot of weight, baker.
